This page is for app builders making data-modeling decisions. It explains what
each [collection](/build/collections/) actually costs — in CPU and, more
importantly, in **disk reads** — so you can choose a shape that stays fast as
your state grows.

Throughout, `n` is the number of entries in the collection you are operating on,
`k` is the number of results a query returns, and `K` is the number of
**siblings under one parent** (for a top-level collection, `K` is that
collection's own entry count).

## How storage actually works (and why it matters for perf)

Calimero state is not an in-memory `HashMap`. It is a content-addressed tree of
storage entities, and three properties of that tree drive every number below:

1. **Each logical entry is its own storage entity.** A map with `n` keys is `n`
   separate records on disk, each addressed by a content id. The parent
   collection stores only the **set of child ids**, not the values.

2. **There is no value index.** Nothing maps a value (or a key's position) to
   where it lives, beyond the parent's child-id set. So to read every entry, you
   must do `n` point reads — one round-trip to the backend per entry. Iteration
   is inherently `O(n)` reads; there is no cheaper path.

3. **Every write re-hashes its siblings.** When you insert or remove an entry,
   the parent re-sorts and SHA-256s **all `K`** of its children to recompute its
   Merkle hash (`index.rs`, `calculate_full_hash_for_children`), then walks the
   ancestor chain to the root doing the same at each level. A write is therefore
   `O(K log K)` in the size of its parent — **not** `O(1)`.

The upside of property 3 is that reading the current root / scope hash is `O(1)`:
it is kept current incrementally by every write, so the cost is paid at write
time, never at read time.

:::caution[Gotcha: writes are not `O(1)`]
Inserting or removing one entry costs `O(K log K)`, where `K` is the number of
siblings under the same parent, because the parent rehashes its entire child set
on every write. A collection with one enormous parent makes every single write
to it slow. Keep `K` bounded — partition large collections (e.g. shard by key
prefix or by time bucket) so no single parent holds the whole dataset.
:::

## Shared primitives

Every collection is built from the same handful of operations. Their costs
compose into the per-collection table further down.

| Primitive | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Derive an entry id | `O(1)` | one SHA-256 over `parent` + key |
| Point read (`get` / `contains`) | `O(1)` in `n` | ~3 backend reads + a borsh decode; independent of collection size |
| Load the child-id set | `O(n)` cold, `O(1)` warm | read the parent's child-id list once, then cache it in memory for the rest of the call |
| `len` | `O(1)` open, `O(n)` guarded | an open collection reads its child trie's count; a guarded one (`Authored*`, `WriteOnce`, `Moderated`, `UserStorage`, anything nested in an owned entry or a cell) loads the entries it admits and counts them |
| Iterate all entries | `O(n)` reads | one point read per entry; there is no value index to shortcut it |
| `insert` / `remove` (any write) | `O(K log K)` + ancestor walk | parent re-sorts and SHA-256s all `K` siblings, then re-hashes each ancestor up to the root |
| Read root / scope hash | `O(1)` | kept current incrementally by every write |

:::note
"Warm" vs "cold" refers to whether the child-id set has already been loaded into
the in-memory cache during the current execution. The **first** access that
needs it pays one `O(n)`-sized read; subsequent accesses in the same call are
free. Neither `len` nor `contains` needs it. A guarded collection cannot count
from its child trie, whose count includes entries the collection does not
admit, so it counts the ones it does admit. The storage crate can keep that
count in an index plane beside the state, but a cluster node keeps no index
plane (see [Ordered reads and indexes](#ordered-reads-and-indexes-on-a-cluster)),
so on a cluster every `len` of a guarded collection loads its entries.
:::

## Per-collection complexity

| Collection | `get` / `contains` | `insert` / `remove` | `len` | Iterate all | Ordered access (range / prefix / page) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `UnorderedMap` / `UnorderedSet` | `O(1)` | `O(K log K)` | `O(1)` warm | `O(n)` reads | **none** — hashed ids have no key order |
| `SortedMap` / `SortedSet` | `O(1)` | `O(K log K)` | `O(1)` warm | `O(n log n)` | every ordered read loads and sorts all entries: `O(n log n)` |
| `IndexedMap` | `O(1)` | `O(K log K)` | `O(1)` warm | `O(n)` reads | every query by **field value** scans all entries: `O(n)` reads |
| `Vector` | `get(i)` is `O(i)` reads | `push` `O(K log K)`; `update(i)` `O(1)` | `O(1)` warm | `O(n)` reads | positional only — see gotcha |
| `ReplicatedGrowableArray` (RGA) | `get_text` `O(n log n)` | single-char `insert` `O(n log n)`; `insert_str` is bulk | `O(n log n)` | `O(n log n)` | n/a |
| `FugueText` | `get_text` / `char_at` `O(b)` in blocks | writes each touched block once; `insert_str` and `apply_delta` are bulk | `O(b)` | `O(b)` | n/a |
| `Counter` / `PNCounter` | `value()` `O(actors)` reads | `increment` `O(K log K)` | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| `LwwRegister` | `O(1)` | `O(K log K)` | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| `Authored*` (map / vector) | same as the underlying collection, plus a per-entry owner-stamp read | | `O(n)`: loads the admitted entries (see the note above) | | |

A few rows deserve their own warnings.

### `Vector`

`Vector` keeps insertion order, but it is backed by the same child-id set as
every other collection — it is **not** an array you can index into in constant
time.

- `push` mints a random element id (so it skips the per-key id hash), but it is
  still a write, so it pays the `O(K log K)` parent rehash like everything else.
- `update(i)` is `O(1)`: it looks the id up by position in the cached child-id
  set, then does one point write.
- `get(i)` is `O(i)` **reads**: it iterates entries from the start and loads
  each one until it reaches index `i`, discarding the rest.

:::caution[Gotcha: `Vector::get(i)` is `O(index)`, not `O(1)`]
Reading `vec.get(i)` loads and decodes `i + 1` entries to return one. A loop of
`for i in 0..len { vec.get(i) }` is therefore `O(n^2)` reads. To read a vector in
order, **iterate it** (`vec.iter()`, a single `O(n)` pass) instead of indexing
by position.
:::

### Ordered reads and indexes on a cluster

`SortedMap`, `SortedSet` and `IndexedMap` are written to use an ordered index
plane (the `storage_index_*` host functions) beside the app's state, so a range,
a prefix or a query by field value could seek instead of scan. A cluster node
does not keep that plane (its state store implements none of it), so the
collections fall back to reading every entry, on every read:

- `SortedMap` / `SortedSet`: `range`, `prefix`, `page`, `first`, `last`,
  `entries()`, `keys()` and `values()` load all entries and sort them in
  memory, `O(n log n)` after `O(n)` reads.
- `IndexedMap`: `query(index).eq(v)`, `.range(a..b)`, `.desc().limit(k)` and
  `.count()` load all entries and filter them, `O(n)` reads.

The answers are correct; they are not cheap. Keep a collection you read in
order or query by field small, or shard it (below) so each read covers one
shard. `IndexedMap`'s stored bytes are exactly an `UnorderedMap`'s, so
switching an existing field between the two needs no migration.

### `ReplicatedGrowableArray` (RGA)

Each RGA operation re-materializes the whole document — a depth-first walk plus a
sort over all visible characters (`O(n log n)`) — to resolve the current text
order. That cost is per *call*, not per character.

:::caution[Gotcha: single-char `insert` re-materializes the whole document]
`rga.insert(pos, ch)` rebuilds the entire ordered document (`O(n log n)`) on
**every** call, so typing `m` characters one at a time is `O(m * n log n)`. To
add a string, call `insert_str` once: it materializes the order a single time
and then appends each character. Same applies to reading — call `get_text()`
once and slice the result rather than calling it in a loop.
:::

### Collaborative text

`FugueText` stores text as blocks of up to 256 consecutive characters, and a read rebuilds the order from those blocks, so it costs `O(b)` in blocks rather than in characters.
Text typed or pasted in one place fills a block before opening the next; text inserted in many scattered places makes more, smaller blocks, up to one per character in the worst case.
A write stores each block it touches once, so one `apply_delta` for a whole editor change costs one write per touched block rather than one per character.
`RichText` adds one row per formatting mark and nothing for a mark already in effect, and `RichDocument` writes a constant number of rows to insert or move a block however long the document is.
The measured rows for every text workload, RGA included, are pinned in [`tools/storage-cost/storage-costs.json`](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/blob/master/tools/storage-cost/storage-costs.json); see [benchmarking](https://github.com/calimero-network/core/blob/master/docs/benchmarking.md) to rerun them.

### `Counter`

A counter stores one slot per executor that has touched it. `value()` reads
**every** slot and sums them, so it is `O(actors)` reads — cheap while a handful
of accounts write to it, linear in the number of distinct writers over the
counter's lifetime.

## Replication cost

A call runs once, on the app's leader; the other replicas apply the keys and
values the run wrote and run nothing ([The write path](/protocol/write-path/)).
So what a call costs the cluster is its write set: the entries it touched plus
the parent hashes it recomputed, all paid once, on the leader. Nothing is
merged between replicas, and a replica that falls behind catches up by applying
the same entries.

## Blobs

Large binary payloads use the [blob store](/protocol/blobs/), which is separate
from the collection tree:

- Content is split into fixed **1 MiB chunks**.
- A multi-chunk blob's `BlobId` is `SHA-256` over its **child chunk ids**, not
  over the raw content.
- Reading a blob is `O(chunks)` — it streams chunk by chunk.

Blobs are the right home for anything large or opaque (files, media,
serialized snapshots). Storing big values as collection entries instead forces
that data through the per-entry read and sibling-rehash machinery above.

## Worked example: a chat that doesn't shard

Make the write-cost cliff concrete. A chat app stores every message as a direct
child of one map:

```rust
// All messages under a single parent — K grows without bound.
messages: UnorderedMap<u64, LwwRegister<String>>,
```

By message 100,000, `K ≈ 100_000`. Each new message is an `insert`, and every
insert re-sorts and SHA-256s **all** of the parent's children to recompute its
Merkle hash — `O(K log K)`. So the 100,000th message hashes ~100k siblings, the
room gets *slower the more it is used*. This is a write cliff, not a read
problem — point reads stay `O(1)`.

The fix is to bound `K`: shard the messages so no single parent holds the whole
history. Bucketing by UTC day keeps each parent at one day's traffic, and the
inner `SortedMap` gives ordered reads within a day, sorting only that day:

```rust
// "room:2026-06-25" -> that day's messages, time-ordered. Each parent's K is
// one day of traffic (thousands), not the lifetime total (hundreds of thousands).
messages: UnorderedMap<String, SortedMap<[u8; 8], LwwRegister<String>>>,
```

| | One flat map | Sharded by day |
|---|---|---|
| Parent size `K` at 100k messages | ~100,000 | ~one day's count |
| Cost of the next `insert` | `O(100k · log 100k)` | `O(day · log day)` |
| Ordered read of one day | sorts the whole history | sorts one day |

The shard key is whatever bounds growth for *your* access pattern — a time
bucket, a room id, a key prefix, or an owner. The only requirement is that no
single parent grows unbounded.

## Practical guidance

- **Use the right collection for the access pattern.** Point lookups →
  `UnorderedMap`. Ordered scans, ranges, or pagination → `SortedMap`. Append-log
  with in-order reads → `Vector` (iterate, don't index). Collaborative text →
  `FugueText` with one `apply_delta` per editor change. A running total across writers → `Counter`.
- **Reach for `SortedMap` only when you need order.** On a cluster every
  ordered read sorts the whole collection, so keep it small or sharded.
- **Build RGA text with `insert_str`, never a per-character loop.** One bulk call
  materializes the document order once instead of once per character.
- **Don't iterate to compute what you can track incrementally.** Iterating to
  count, sum, or find a max is `O(n)` reads every time. If you need a running
  aggregate, maintain it as you write (e.g. a `Counter` or a dedicated field)
  rather than recomputing it on read.
- **Iterate vectors; never index them in a loop.** `vec.iter()` is one `O(n)`
  pass; `for i in 0..len { vec.get(i) }` is `O(n^2)` reads.
- **Watch write cost on large parents.** Because every write rehashes its
  siblings, a single collection holding tens of thousands of entries makes every
  write to it slow. Partition large datasets
  (shard by key prefix, time bucket, or owner) so no single parent grows
  unbounded.

For the storage tree underneath these costs, see
[Collections](/build/collections/) and [CRDT internals](/protocol/crdt-internals/).
